en: Then, at the forefront of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, Draupadī—her garments and hair seized by Duḥśāsana—cried out, having no other protector: "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (1)

O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, O enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, O compassionate one toward devotees, O Blessed One, O Murāri! Protect me, O Keśava, O Lord of the worlds, O Govinda, O Dāmodara, O Mādhava! || 2 ||

It is said that a cowherd girl, desiring to sell her goods yet with her mental faculties entirely fixed upon the feet of the Enemy of Mura, addressed the curds and other items out of delusion, saying, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (3)
In the mortars, the bewildered cowherd girls, pounding the gathered rice with pestles, sing out with born affection: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava!"
A certain lotus-eyed woman was teaching a pet parrot, whose beak was as red as a *kiṃśuka* flower, resting within the hollow of her lotus-hand: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (5)
In every house, the groups of cowherd women have begun at every moment to teach the yellowish-green parrots to speak with faltering voices: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava!"
As all the cowherd girls lulled the prince—who was reclining on his couch—to sleep, they sang a musical composition set to specific notes and rhythms, calling out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava!"
A cowherd woman, taking a ball of fresh butter, called out to the child Rāmānuja—who was restless with the play of his glances—as he was still a mere infant: "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (8)
O royal swan upon the lotus-face, delighting in ornaments of variegated colors, ever speak the words "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava" upon my tongue, the foremost stage.
Yaśodā joyfully addressed him—who was seated upon her hip, embraced by the child, sucking at her breast, and the sole beloved of Lakṣmī—saying, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (10).
While his own self was playing within the cow-pen, equal in age to the cowherd boys, Yaśodā called out to Kṛṣṇa with affection, saying, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (11)
Bound tightly by Yaśodā with a mortar using a rope made from cow-throat grass, he who eats fresh butter wept softly, crying out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (12)

In her own courtyard, a cowherd woman, seizing a ball of fresh butter that was eager for play with her bangles, crushed it with the palm of her hand while crying out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (13)
In every house, all the groups of cowherd women, having gathered together in a great assembly, constantly recite his auspicious names: "Govinda," "Dāmodara," and "Mādhava. (14)

At the foot of the *mandāra* tree, with a face beautiful to behold and lips like the bimba fruit, filling the air with the sound of his flute; standing in the midst of the cows, cowherds, and cowherd girls—[I call upon you] as Govinda, Dāmodara, and Mādhava! (15)
Having risen at the end of the night and remembering the childhood play of Yaśodā’s son, the cowherd women sing aloud while churning curds: "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (16)
Then, having eaten the lump of butter given to him, Yaśodā, feeling suspicious in her home, said: "Tell the truth, O Murāri! Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (17)
Having worshipped the house, the young woman, her stream of love overflowing, churned the curd; then the gopīs, together with their companions, sang, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (18).

In some places at dawn, having placed a churning-stick into a vessel filled with curd, a young woman gazes upon Mukunda and performs various songs, crying out, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (19).
Desiring his welfare, Yaśodā—her eyes overflowing with love—called her son, who was intent on play, for the sake of food and bathing, saying, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (20)

While Viṣṇu was lying comfortably in his abode, the chief divine sages and munis took refuge in him, addressing him as "O Acyuta," "O Govinda," "O Dāmodara," and "O Mādhava"; through this, they attained absorption in him.
Having abandoned sleep at the break of dawn and performed their duties, the foremost of Brahmins constantly recite at the conclusion of the Vedas: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (22)
In Vṛndāvana, the cowherds and cowherd girls, seeing Rādhā distressed by separation from Govinda, sang with tearful eyes: "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (23)
As the cows returned from their grazing at dawn, Yaśodā gently awakened her son with the palm of her hand, calling out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (24).
With long hair possessing the beauty of coral, their bodies purified by subsisting on wind, water, and leaves, the sages recite at the roots of the trees: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (25)
Speaking thus, the women of Vraja, deeply distressed by separation and with their minds intensely fixed on Kṛṣṇa, cast aside all shame and wept aloud, crying, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (26)
Once, a gopī began to recite these words to a parrot perched upon a jeweled cage: "O root of bliss, moon of Vraja, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (27)
Holding the chin of the lotus-petal-eyed one as he was tying a tuft of hair with cow-tail hair, his mother said, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (28)
At the time of dawn, the multitude of excellent cowherds, holding staffs of cane for the sake of guarding the cattle, called out to the infinite, primordial one: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (29)
When Murāri descended from the Kadamba tree into the lake to subdue Kāliya, the cowherd women and the cowherds came running and cried out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (30)
When Mukunda reached Akrūra and entered Mathurā for the festival of the bow, he was addressed by the citizens as "Victory!", and called "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (31).
As soon as the two sons of Vasudeva were led away from the heart of Vṛndāvana by Kaṃsa’s messenger, the cowherd woman wept in the middle of her house, crying out, “Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (32)
Seeing the son of Yaśodā, bound by the serpent Kāliya in the lake, the cowherd boys rolled along the path crying out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (33).
Beholding the Lord of the Yadu clan departing for Mathurā in Akrūra’s chariot, the cowherd boys, due to their separation from him, cried out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (34)
Lying upon a bed of flowers at the edge of the lotus grove, deprived of Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd girl cried out with her eyes like blossoming blue lotuses: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (35)
Surrounded by her parents, Gopī entered the house and lamented: "O Viśvanātha, Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! Come and protect me! (36)
Having quickly perceived Hari to be in Vṛndāvana, a certain gopī went to the forest at night; not seeing him there either, she spoke out of extreme fear: "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (37)
Even while lying comfortably in their own homes, those mortals who utter the names of Viṣṇu—calling out "Govinda," "Dāmodara," and "Mādhava"—will certainly attain absorption in Him. (38)

Beholding Rādhā, whose eyes were like lotuses and who was distressed by separation from Govinda, that friend, her own eyes like full-blown blue lotuses, wept, crying out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (39)
O tongue, knower of tastes, you who are fond of sweetness—I tell you the truth for your ultimate benefit: you should utter sweet syllables, saying "Govinda," "Dāmodara," and "Mādhava. (40)
Those who know the Vedas declare that Govinda, Dāmodara, and Mādhava are the physicians for humanity who remove disease forever, and the seed that destroys the threefold afflictions of saṃsāra. (41)
When Rāmacandra, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, departed for the depths of the forest at his father’s command, Rāma’s own mother wailed out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (42).
Being led away from the depths of the Daṇḍaka forest by the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, Sītā, who had no other protector, then cried out: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (43)
Separated from Rāma, that daughter of Janaka, contemplating the form of Rāma within her heart, wept, crying out: "O Lord of the Raghus, protect me! O Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (44)
"Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Raghu dynasty, cause of the happiness and sorrow of both gods and demons! Sītā wept in the midst of the ocean, crying out, 'O Govinda, O Dāmodara, O Mādhava! (45)
With his foot seized by a crocodile within the water, having abandoned all his distressed kinsmen, the lordly elephant then cried out intensely: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (46)
Haṃsadhvaja, accompanied by Śaṅkha, saw his son falling into the cauldron while chanting the holy names of Hari: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (47)
Having heeded the words of Durvāsas, Kṛṣṇā spoke to the lord dwelling in the forest; having entered within him with her mind, she offered oblations, calling out, "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (48).

He who is immeasurable, the remover of anxiety, and the wish-fulfilling Pārijāta tree for those who think of him—He who is dark-hued like musk—should always be meditated upon by yogis as Govinda, Dāmodara, and Mādhava. (49)

O Viṣṇu, O Govinda, O Dāmodara, O Mādhava, grant me a hand to hold as I have fallen into the bottomless well of saṃsāra, which is filled with the darkness of delusion and scorched by the objects of the senses.
I entreat only you: O tongue, when the Wielder of the Staff, the End-maker (Kṛtānta), has arrived, speak these very sweet words with true devotion: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (51)

O tongue that perceives flavors, worship this easily accessible and pleasing mantra for liberation from the bonds of existence—the mantra "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava," which was recited by sages such as Dvaipāyana.
O Gopāla, O Vaṃśīdhara, O Ocean of Beauty, O Lord of the World, O Nārāyaṇa, O Friend of the Wretched! Always utter these names in loud tones: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! (53)
O tongue, always worship these beautiful and heart-stealing names of Kṛṣṇa, which destroy all the afflictions of his devotees: "Govinda," "Dāmodara," and "Mādhava. (54)
Govinda, Govinda, Hare, Murāri; Govinda, Govinda, Mukunda, Kṛṣṇa; Govinda, Govinda, O you whose hand holds the discus; Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! || 55 ||

At the end of happiness, this alone is the essence; at the end of suffering, this alone is what should be sung; at the end of the body, this alone is what should be chanted: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (56)
Having been seized by those irresistible words, Kṛṣṇā, like a frightened doe, somehow or other entered the assembly hall; there, she mentally invoked Govinda, Dāmodara, and Mādhava.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Beloved of Rādhā, O Lord of Gokula, O Gopāla, O Lord of Govardhana, O Viṣṇu! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (58)
O Śrīnātha, Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe! O Śrī Devakīnandana, enemy of the Daityas! O tongue, drink only this nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (59)
O Lord of the Gopīs, O Enemy of Kaṃsa, O Mukunda, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Keśava, O Vāsudeva! O tongue, drink only this nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (60)
O delighter of the cowherd folk, Lord of Vraja, who entered the forest for the purpose of tending the cattle—O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (51)
O Lord of Life, Sustainer of the Universe, Slayer of Kaiṭabha, Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa, Wielder of the Discus! O tongue, drink only this nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (62)
O Hare, O Murāri, O Madhusūdana, O Śrī Rāma, O Consort of Sītā, O Enemy of Rāvaṇa! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (53)

O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava"—you who are the lotus-eyed one who supports the mountain of the illustrious Lord of the Yādavas, and who are skilled in bestowing happiness upon the cows, the cowherds, and the gopīs. 64.

O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava"—He who, assuming the guise of a cowherd to lift the burden of the earth, performed the pastimes of a friend and remained as the final refuge. 65.
O tongue, you who are skilled in destroying Baka, Baka, Aghāsura, Dhenuka, Keśī, and Tṛṇāvarta, drink this very nectar: "Govinda! Dāmodara! Mādhava! 66.
O Śrī Jānakī, O Jīvana, O Rāmacandra, O Enemy of the Night-stalkers, O Lord of Bharata’s elder brother! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (67)
O Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, Hari, Nṛsiṃha, O remover of Prahlāda’s distress, O Merciful One! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (68)
O you who possess a form immortal despite the appearance of a playful human, O you whose majesty has made all kings your servants—O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (69)
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Hare, Murāri! O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! (70)
Though capable of speaking, no one speaks; oh, the inclination of people toward calamity! O tongue, drink this very nectar: "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava! 71.
Thus ends the Śrī Govindadāmodarastotra composed by the venerable Bilvamaṅgalācārya.
